sections.html:
East-central Nebraska holds Platte County, with Columbus as its seat. The Platte River forms the southern edge, and the Loup River drops through the lower half before meeting the Platte just outside Columbus. Most of the land is low, rolling farm ground.

Humphrey and a slice of Newman Grove are the other cities. Villages include Cornlea, Creston, Duncan, Lindsay, Monroe, Platte Center and Tarnov, and Lakeview is a census-designated place. Every address is billed by the same treasurer, though the school and city levies stacked on each statement change from town to town.

Population was 34,296 at the 2020 census and an estimated 35,649 in 2025. The county has 13,313 households and 14,094 housing units, and median household income was $71,552 in the 2024 estimate. Work in Columbus centers on farming and factories. When an employer moves someone out of town, a house can need a buyer fast, and those owners usually value a certain closing day over a long listing.

sections.h2: Who bills and collects the tax
sections.html:
Columbus is home to the treasurer, who bills and collects every real estate and personal property tax in Platte County. Find the office on the first floor, west side, of the courthouse at 2610 14th Street, or phone 402-563-4913. It opens Monday through Friday at 8:00 a.m. and closes at 5:00 p.m., with a later 8:30 start on the second Thursday of each month.

You can pay through Nebraska Taxes Online, send a check, or drop one in the box at the west entrance. Credit cards add 2.49 percent, and debit cards add $2.95. Statements go out from late November through December, so if yours has not appeared, ring the office instead of waiting.

StepDate or rule
Taxes dueDecember 31
First half delinquentThe following May 1
Second half delinquentThe following September 1
Interest on delinquent tax14 percent statutory rate
Valuation protest filingOn or before June 30, with the County Clerk
Appeal of a board decisionTax Equalization and Review Commission, by August 24

On its page the treasurer posts a Delinquent Tax Listing and a levy booklet showing the rate set by each taxing district. If your bill looks higher than a friend's in another town, the booklet usually explains it.

Think of the tax year as two clocks. The first runs from the December statement to the May delinquency date, and the second from May to the September date. A house that closes in between should have a title company that knows which half is already settled.

A protest starts with Form 422, filed with the County Clerk by June 30. Use a separate form for every parcel. The clerk routes it to the County Board of Equalization, which schedules a hearing.

The form has to name the reason for the protest, the value you think is right, and enough paperwork for the board to arrive at a different figure. If it is missing any of those, or if it comes in after June 30, the board dismisses it. By August 2 the clerk mails you the decision. Still unhappy? The state commission takes appeals filed on or before August 24.

Useful evidence includes a recent appraisal, a contractor's estimate for repairs you have put off, and sale prices of comparable houses nearby. The same form also works when the assessor adds property that was left off the rolls or imposes a penalty.

School levy follows the district. Columbus Public Schools (District 1) and Lakeview Community Schools (District 5) cover much of the area. Humphrey Public Schools (District 67) and Newman Grove Public Schools (District 13) serve the north and west. Twin River Public Schools in Genoa, Leigh Community Schools, Clarkson Public Schools, St. Edward Public Schools and Madison Public Schools also reach in.

Look for the district code printed on your statement before you compare your tax with a neighbor's.

Roofs, gutters and basement drainage take a beating in summer storms, and a house close to the Loup or Platte should get a flood check before it is listed. Flooding in 2019 reached Columbus. Put repair records, insurance claims and any elevation papers in a single folder, so a buyer's questions about water get quick, specific answers.

The county holds a tax sale every March for unpaid real estate tax. Investors buy the overdue amount as a certificate. They do not buy your house. Even so, a delinquent bill is more than a penalty: it starts a countdown. Pay the balance, or close a sale before sale day, and the exposure is gone.

Rules for the sale and the delinquent listing are on the treasurer's page, so you can check whether your parcel appears there.

Your first call should be to the treasurer for the balance on the parcel, because title companies insist that back taxes be cleared at closing. Next, set aside money for the deed tax. Nebraska's documentary stamp tax is the seller's to pay, the register of deeds collects it, and the rate is $3.32 on each $1,000 of value for deeds recorded from July 18, 2026. Form 521, the Real Estate Transfer Statement, goes in with the deed.

Typical sellers in this spot own an inherited house, a rental with a tenant, or a place with repairs half done. Buyers paying cash need no loan approval and no lender appraisal, which is why those closings can be quick. Send us the address if you would like a plain description of how a sale would go.

sections.h2: What to bring to the treasurer or title company
sections.html: A modest folder spares you return trips: your parcel number, photo ID, older statements you still have, and proof of authority if an estate holds the house. With a mortgage in place, also request a payoff letter so the closing agent can add the tax balance and give you one clear total.

Quick sales around Columbus and the smaller towns tend to follow one short path.

  • You give us the address and a few facts about the house, plus any tax or lien balance.
  • A buyer reviews the place and offers cash, with no bank in the middle.
  • The title company starts its search and asks the treasurer for the balance.
  • At the table you sign the deed and Form 521, and the stamp tax comes out of your proceeds.

With so few steps, the schedule follows title work and the speed of the tax payoff, not a lender's calendar.

faqs.q: When are Platte County property taxes due?
faqs.a: December 31. The first half is delinquent the following May 1 and the second half the following September 1, and late tax draws 14 percent interest.

faqs.q: Where do I file a Platte County valuation protest?
faqs.a: With the County Clerk in Columbus, on Form 422, on or before June 30. Each parcel gets its own protest with the reason, the value you want and supporting documents.

faqs.q: Can I pay Platte County taxes online?
faqs.a: Yes, through Nebraska Taxes Online. Mail and the courthouse drop box by the west entrance also work. Credit cards add 2.49 percent and debit cards $2.95.

faqs.q: What is the Platte County Treasurer's phone number?
faqs.a: 402-563-4913. The office is at 2610 14th Street in Columbus, open weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.

faqs.q: Who pays the deed tax on a Platte County sale?
faqs.a: You do, as seller. The register of deeds takes the stamp tax when the deed is recorded, with a rate of $3.32 per $1,000 of value from July 18, 2026.
